common_misconceptions.misconception: Students label a sport 'aerobic' or 'anaerobic' without anchoring to intensity and duration. The Edexcel mark scheme expects justified reasoning ('100m sprint, ~10s at maximal intensity, insufficient oxygen reaching working muscles -> anaerobic'). Generic 'because it's short' answers lose marks.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Physical Education teacher support (https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-gcses/physical-education-2016.html)

common_misconceptions.topic: Lever diagrams — load, fulcrum, effort order
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mis-order LFE when drawing or labelling levers, especially the third-class lever (effort between fulcrum and load — applies to the bicep curl). Mark schemes require the correct visual ordering on labelled diagrams. The 'F-L-E / L-F-E / E-F-L is wrong' framing fails because Edexcel insists on the middle component identifying the class (1st = F middle, 2nd = L middle, 3rd = E middle).

Students confuse the open-closed continuum with basic-complex or low-organisation/high-organisation. Edexcel uses THREE separate continua (basic/complex, open/closed, low-org/high-org) — they are not synonymous. Open = environment changes (football pass under pressure); complex = many decisions/moving parts (gymnastics routine); high-org = subroutines hard to separate (golf swing). A skill can be high on one continuum and low on another.

Students write SMART targets that are not actually measurable or time-bound ('get better at football this term'). Mark schemes credit only targets that are simultaneously specific (named skill), measurable (number/percentage), achievable, realistic (relative to current ability) and time-bound (a deadline). Edexcel uses 'achievable' for A, not 'accepted'.

Students treat the 9-mark question as a description task — they list facts about both topics but don't link, evaluate or apply to sporting context. Edexcel's Evaluate command word requires a supported judgement; the rubric rewards (a) range, (b) balance (advantages and disadvantages), (c) sporting application throughout, (d) conclusion. One-sided answers cap at level 1.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel 1PE0 specification Appendix 6 Command Word Taxonomy (https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-gcses/physical-education-2016.html)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students extract a single number from a graph without saying what it shows or comparing it. Edexcel mark schemes for Interpret Data questions credit: (1) quote a figure with units, (2) make a comparison or trend statement, (3) explain the sporting implication. Naming the trend without a number, or quoting a number without context, both lose a mark.

student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Evaluate: Edexcel's single 9-mark question on Component 2 expects synthesis of sport psychology AND socio-cultural content. Students often answer only one topic. Force a 'For… However…' structure with a sporting example and a conclusion sentence. Mark scheme: level 1 (1-3) = limited, level 2 (4-6) = developed one-sided, level 3 (7-9) = balanced + applied + concluded.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Assess: Edexcel's Assess command word requires REASONED ARGUMENT to reach a judgement on the relative importance of factors. Students often describe factors without weighing them. Teach: identify the factors, compare them, conclude with a ranking and a reason.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Analyse: Students list rather than analyse. Each point should be: state the factor, link to performance, give a sporting example. Avoid bullet-point answers; the mark scheme rewards continuous prose with sporting application.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Discuss: Edexcel's Discuss requires exploring DIFFERENT or CONTRASTING viewpoints (advantages and disadvantages). Single-sided discussions cap at half marks. Teach 'On one hand… on the other…' as scaffolding.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Explain: Students give the WHAT without the WHY. Edexcel mark schemes for Explain reward 'fact… because… therefore…' chains of reasoning. State the point, give the reason, state the consequence.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Calculate: Students forget units (bpm, %, ml, seconds) or skip working. Mark schemes typically award 1 for correct working, 1 for the answer with units. CO = SV × HR style calculations are likely in Component 1 — show all three steps.
student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Identify: Students give two answers when one is required, hedging. Mark schemes typically take the FIRST answer — extra answers can be ignored or, if contradictory, lose the mark. Teach: pick one, commit.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 1 (Fitness and Body Systems) is 36% of the qualification and 80 marks. Applied anatomy and physiology + Physical training dominate. Section A focuses on Topics 1-2, Section B on Topic 3, Section C is the single extended-response question. Use of data is embedded across all sections.

Component 2 (Health and Performance) is 24% of the qualification and 60 marks. Section A is Topic 1 (health/wellbeing/diet), Section B is Topics 2 and 3 (sport psychology and socio-cultural). Section C is a single 9-mark extended response linking sport psychology AND socio-cultural — a synoptic synthesis. This is unique to Edexcel.

Use of Data (Topic 4) does NOT have its own section in either paper — it is embedded throughout. Every lesson should include at least one Interpret Data, Calculate or original-data flavoured question where the content is amenable. Data fluency is a high-volume mark-earning skill.

Practical NEA (Components 3 and 4) is 30% + 10% of the qualification and is teacher-assessed. This revision platform does not address it. The 30 lessons cover 100% of the assessable theory content (60% of the qualification grade).
current_spec_changes: Specification Issue 5 (September 2024) is the current authoritative document. The only change between Issue 4 and Issue 5 is a typographic correction on the NEA activity list (inline / roller hockey — slash removed). No content additions or removals affect Paper 1 or Paper 2 for the 2026 series. Source: https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-gcses/physical-education-2016.html
pedagogical_notes: EEF retrieval-practice guidance: real retrieval (free recall, blank-page brain dumps, low-stakes quizzing) outperforms re-reading. Knowledge checks and flashcards in this build must require active recall, not recognition — phrase flashcard questions to elicit a definition rather than a multiple choice. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-not-another-quiz-refining-retrieval-practice

EEF cognitive science review: dual coding (words paired with imagery) is high-utility but free-tier lessons cannot embed generated diagrams. Where a diagram would clarify (heart chambers, lever systems, planes/axes), the prose must do the imaging work — describe the anatomy precisely AND include a 'sketch this without looking' retrieval prompt. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/evidence-reviews/cognitive-science-approaches-in-the-classroom

EEF spaced-practice principle: revisit material across days. Lessons should cross-reference earlier content explicitly (when teaching long-term effects in L9, retrieve the cardiovascular response from L5 and respiratory response from L6). This builds the synoptic understanding that Edexcel's 9-mark question demands. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-putting-cognitive-science-principles-into-practice

EEF interleaving: mixing related topics in retrieval forces discrimination. Component 2 knowledge checks should mix sport psychology with socio-cultural content — Edexcel rewards this synthesis directly via the 9-mark question. Component 1 should mix anatomy with training. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-the-abc-of-cognitive-science

Glossary terms: PE is terminology-dense. Aim for at least 6 inline glossary terms per lesson; 8-10 is realistic in anatomy-heavy lessons. Definitions one sentence, reusable across lessons. The Edexcel Appendix 5 glossary of key terms is a useful checklist (no need to copy verbatim — paraphrase).

Edexcel command words: Edexcel uses Assess, Analyse, Calculate, Classify, Complete, Define, Describe, Discuss, Examine, Explain, Evaluate, Give, Identify, Justify, Label, Predict, Select, State. Practice questions must match these command words. Avoid AQA's 'Analyse' phrasing when the Edexcel equivalent is 'Assess' or 'Examine'.

Data interpretation: Edexcel Topic 4 is embedded across BOTH papers. Generate original fictional data tables and graph descriptions — never reproduce real Sport England, NHS or Edexcel figures. Use realistic numbers (e.g. 'Sarah's heart rate during a 30-minute run: rest 70 bpm, peak 165 bpm, recovery 90 bpm at 5 min'). Include at least one Interpret Data or Calculate question per lesson where the content is amenable.

Mark scheme rubric: StudyVault uses Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging on 6- and 9-mark levels-based questions. NEVER use 'Level 1/2/3', 'Nothing worthy of credit' or 'Award X marks for Y' (the validator bans the 'Award N marks for' pattern). Phrase mark allocations as '1 mark for X; 1 mark for Y' or 'Up to 3 marks: identification (1), reasoning (1), application (1)'.

Plain-text fields (description, practice_questions[].text/.type/.marks, knowledge_checks[].q, flashcard_questions[].q/.a, glossary_terms[].term/.definition) MUST use plain unicode (apostrophes, en-dashes, em-dashes typed directly). NEVER use HTML entities such as ’, &, – in these fields — entities are only allowed inside content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html.

Copyright: do not include spec codes (1PE0), component codes (1PE0/01, 1PE0/02), section labels, or Edexcel trademark question stems verbatim. Do not reproduce Edexcel mark scheme phrasing. Build generic GCSE-level questions with our 13 registered command-word types.

Knowledge check shape: use `correct: <int>` (integer index) plus `options: [string, string, ...]` — NEVER write `answers: [...]` (text-array shape). The quick-quiz player breaks silently on the wrong shape. (Validator catches it pre-insert but content agents have hallucinated this before.)
